passage:
Pankaj counted the weeks to the exam on his fingers, then took away the weeks for going over old topics and mock tests. What remained, divided by the syllabus blocks, gave him a handful of days per block, far too few. Something had to be cut. He laid out five years of past papers and saw that two topics carried most of the marks, while three were asked once in a while. He started with the big ones and left the rare ones for last.

Lokesh, in the same coaching centre, joined eleven chat groups, downloaded dozens of PDFs and changed teachers twice in a month. He felt busy all day. When Pankaj asked which book he had finished, Lokesh scratched his head. None.

Pranav studied late every night for two weeks, and his mock scores fell. He looked at the dates and saw that the dips followed the sleepless stretches. He set fixed sleep hours, a short walk each evening and one free evening a week. Three weeks later his answers were more accurate.

qa.q: How many chat groups did Lokesh join?
How did Pankaj's approach to the syllabus differ from Lokesh's?
qa.a: Pankaj counted his time and used past papers to start with the topics carrying most of the marks, while Lokesh collected groups, PDFs and teachers and finished no book.

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling when asked which book he had finished?
qa.a: Embarrassed and a little uneasy, shown by scratching his head.
Lokesh could pick one book and one teacher, finish it chapter by chapter, and use past papers to see what matters.

grounding: Four approaches to preparing for a competitive exam: working backward, prioritising by marks, collecting resources instead of studying, and planning around slumps.
